summary_html: Case results in **child fatality or serious injury**, triggering mandatory federal and state review. Data and lessons inform systemic reform.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — establishes national commission and reporting requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure and case review of fatalities

primary_citations.citation_text: Pennsylvania - Title 23 Pa.C.S. Chapter 63 (Child Protective Services Law)
Pennsylvania - 42 Pa.C.S. Chapter 63 (Juvenile Act – dependency proceedings)
Title 23: Domestic Relations - CHILD WELFARE PRIMARY

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the dependency adjudication of a child certified as a near fatality, holding the trial court did not abuse its discretion where medical evidence established extensive inflicted injuries and the mother failed to seek treatment.
key_cases.relevance: A published Pennsylvania decision addressing a formally certified near fatality.
key_cases.quote: In order to adjudicate a child dependent, the court must determine that the above definition has been met by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and reinstating the trial court, the court held that the rebuttable presumption of 23 Pa.C.S. § 6381(d) identifying the caregiver as the abuser applies even where a child was in the care of multiple responsible adults.
key_cases.relevance: Applies to serious-injury cases where the agency can prove abuse but not who inflicted it.
key_cases.quote: when a child is in the care of multiple parents or other persons responsible for care, those individuals are accountable for the care and protection of the child

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court held that placing a child in state-regulated foster care creates a special relationship imposing affirmative constitutional duties, but affirmed summary judgment because the caseworker's conduct amounted at most to negligence and did not shock the conscience.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the culpability standard for constitutional claims when a child is harmed while in care.
key_cases.quote: when the state places a child in state-regulated foster care, the state has entered into a special relationship with that child which imposes upon it certain affirmative duties

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative constitutional duty on a child-protection agency to protect a child from private violence where the child remains in the parent's custody rather than in state custody.
key_cases.relevance: The threshold rule for constitutional liability when a child known to the agency is killed or seriously injured at home.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

state_agency.name: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, Office of Children, Youth, and Families

extended_foster_care_age: Up to age 21, conditional: adjudicated dependent before 18, youth requests the court to retain jurisdiction, and meets one of five activity conditions; re-entry may be requested before 21 (42 Pa.C.S. §§ 6302, 6351(j))

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason
